summary:
AMC (Allied Mastercomputer) is an offline health monitoring system for long-duration missions. It runs on the habitat's own computer, gathers health indicators, compares each astronaut with their own baseline, and says in plain language what their status is and what to do next. A flight surgeon sees the same picture live.

Highlights:
- Rules decide, AI assists: emergencies come from deterministic rules. The local AI only raises flags, with a quote, and never diagnoses.
- 3D body map in a cabin, organs coloured by status.
- Private diary: AI-guided daily talk, day rated green, yellow or red, sealed until landing. Only medical problems leave it.
- Duty roster by energy and morale, cabin control, intercom, simulated space events, sealed AMC Core reports.
- Knowledge base from NASA Human Research Program pages.

Why it fits: radiation is tracked through dosimeter logs; isolation through check-ins, diary and intercom; altered gravity through bone, muscle, heart and eye systems; the closed environment through cabin monitoring and fault alerts. Astronauts see their own status first, even without contact with Earth.

Why it is well made: it works without the AI model, actions are audited, privacy is enforced, and 356 backend and 13 end-to-end tests pass. Data is simulated and thresholds are demo values; it is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AMC (Allied Mastercomputer) is an offline health monitoring and decision-support system for long-duration missions. It runs on one computer in the habitat, with no cloud and no internet link. Astronauts and the flight surgeon each get their own view.

  • Gathers indicators: wearable readings (simulated), sleep, daily check-ins on mood, stress, fatigue and motivation, symptoms, water, exams, notes and a private diary.
  • Compares people with themselves: every reading is judged against that astronaut's own baseline, not a population average.
  • Shows status in plain words: each body system (immune, bone and muscle, cardiovascular, eyes, digestive, respiratory, behavioral) gets a level from "Nothing open" to "Contact now."
  • Advises the astronaut: the local AI companion explains the status and tells the astronaut what to do next, using the mission's protocol steps. It spots symptoms in chat and proposes recording them. It gives motivating wellbeing support, and it adjusts room temperature and light on request. Every piece of advice comes with a reason.
  • Reaches the doctor fast: urgent entries appear on the flight surgeon's console within seconds and wait for approval. Diagnosis and medication decisions stay with the flight surgeon.
  • Keeps safety in rules: severity and emergencies come from deterministic rules. The AI may raise a flag, and only with an exact quote from the astronaut's words.

What benefits does it have?

  • Astronauts can evaluate their own health and get advice on what to do when contact with Earth is slow or lost.
  • Small changes show up early, because alerts follow each person's own normal range.
  • Behavioral health gets real support: a private diary, motivating replies, an intercom and protected rest.
  • The flight surgeon sees one live picture of the whole crew, with every action audited.
  • The system keeps working when the AI model is off.

What is the intended impact?

We want astronauts to be the first line of detection instead of waiting for Earth. We also want health and behavioral risks caught earlier on missions to the Moon and Mars, without giving up crew privacy. The same design could serve other isolated settings, such as polar stations and remote clinics. It is a prototype for now: the data is simulated and nothing is clinically validated.

What tools, languages and software did you use?

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, SQLite, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, three.js (3D body), Recharts, Motion.
  • Local AI: Ollama with Llama 3.1 8B for conversation and nomic-embed-text for knowledge search.
  • Testing: pytest (356 tests) and Playwright (13 end-to-end tests).
  • Knowledge base: NASA Human Research Program risk pages and NASA Technical Reports Server documents.
  • Other tools: Remotion for the demo video, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.
  • Hardware: only an ordinary laptop. The wearable and cabin sensors are simulated.

How is it creative?

  • 3D body in a cabin: organs are coloured by health status inside a model of the crew quarters. Clicking an organ opens that system.
  • A diary that rates the day: the astronaut talks through the day with AMC, and the day is marked green, yellow or red. Only a medical problem leaves the diary, and the doctor cannot read it until the mission returns.
  • Duty roster by energy and morale: AMC shares out station work by how people feel, and states the reason for each assignment.
  • A cabin that listens: "my room is cold" changes the temperature within safe limits. Cabin pressure is never changed without a person.
  • Space events that trigger the real system: solar particle events, link loss, cabin faults and rising vital signs start on a schedule, and AMC's actual reaction is recorded.
  • Two computers, one system: an astronaut on one laptop and the flight surgeon on another exchange data live.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Safety: the AI advises but does not diagnose or prescribe. Urgent symptoms get fixed safety wording and go straight to the doctor.
  • Autonomy: everything works offline, because communication on a long mission can be delayed or lost.
  • Privacy: the diary and AMC's own reports stay sealed until an emergency, with a written reason, or until the mission returns.
  • Honesty about data: every simulated value is labelled SIMULATED and every threshold DEMO. We did not invent medical limits.
  • Real sources: the knowledge base uses NASA material with a record of each source's origin and licence basis.
  • Usability under stress: plain language, one-tap actions, keyboard access, reduced-motion support and phone-width layouts.
  • Languages: the companion understands English and Turkish.
dataRefs: Sibonga, J. D., Spector, E. R., Yardley, G., Alwood, J. S., Myers, J., Evans, H. J., Smith, S. A., & King, L. (2024)
